name: Cinchona bark for fever at Loja
summary: People around Loja in the Andes used cinchona tree bark to cure fevers by about 1630, and the remedy reached Spain around 1640 as a treatment for malaria.
description: Cinchona trees are native to South America, and the article cited calls Loja the axis of the discovery that their bark cures fevers. It concludes that Pedro Leiva, chief at Malacatos near Loja, passed the knowledge to a Jesuit missionary and that it reached the Spanish corregidor around 1630; exports to Spain began around 1640. Most authors it reviews credit the indigenous people with the discovery, but when they made it is disputed.

impact.note: The bark and the quinine isolated from it in 1820 were the main treatment for malaria in many societies on several continents until the twentieth century; it gave a cure for a major disease where there had been none, and alkaloid chemistry and the synthetic antimalarials grew from it.

why: The article quotes an account that people at Malacatos, south of Loja, suffered intermittent fevers and tested plants until they found the bark, and it suggests that earlier experience of treating other local fevers prepared the way.

date.label: c. 1630
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: The article concludes that Chief Leiva revealed the bark's use against fever to a Jesuit missionary and that the knowledge reached the corregidor Juan López Cañizares around 1630.

evidence.supports: Chief Leiva revealed the secret of Cinchona as a febrifuge to a Jesuit missionary and, in turn, shared that information with the Corregidor Juan López Cañizares around 1630.

date.label: 1631 to 1639
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Antonio de la Calancha mentions a fever tree from Loja; the article gives his text the date 1631 in its discussion and 1639 in its list of references.

evidence.supports: said that Antonio de la Calancha (1631) and Sebastiano Bado (1663) mention a “fever tree” from Loja

date.label: c. 1640
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Exports of the bark to Spain began around 1640, according to the diary of Miguel de Santisteban as the article reports it.

evidence.supports: according to the diary of Don Miguel de Santisteban, exports to Spain, which began around 1640, expanded to include Rome and Paris 10 years later
evidence.locator: Section on the trade in the bark, after Figure 2

date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Sebastiano Bado's 1663 text says that powdered bark taken with wine could cure fevers and tertians.

evidence.supports: When two reals of its powder, mixed with wine or another liquid, is ingested, it had the capacity to cure fevers and tertians

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The c. 1630 event is the article's reconstruction from later accounts, not a document of that year; the earliest written mention it reports is Calancha's.

The article calls Nicolas Monardes's 1574 account the oldest reference to indigenous use of a fever bark, but Haggis doubted that such early accounts describe cinchona rather than Myroxylon, and its place is not Loja; it is not an event here.
According to Bado, as the article reports him, the natives learned the remedy between the arrival of the Spaniards and its discovery by Europeans; other authors cited place it in time immemorial.
Francisco Guerra treats Bollo's letter (cited by Bado in 1663) as the oldest written reference; its own date was not established.
The Countess of Chinchón story and the size of the Jesuit role are disputed in the article and are not repeated as fact.
The Palta are named as the discoverers by authors the article cites (Anda Aguirre, Arias), not by a document of the time.

research.note: Cinchona trees are native to South America, the article calls Loja the axis of discovery and says most authors credit the indigenous people as the discoverers, and no earlier use of the bark elsewhere is known; who first found the remedy, and how long before 1630, is disputed.
